headline: Rocky Point blows up: peanut bunker bring bass and blues topside on the new moon push
subhead: The tide finally built like we said it would, and now there's white water off every point from Conimicut to Prudence.
body_markdown:
I was down at the Fields Point pier Tuesday morning watching a guy load his cooler with peanut bunker off a cast net, and he looks up at me and says, "Vinny, there's fish crashing this stuff all the way out past Rocky Point." I didn't need him to tell me twice. I've been chasing peanut schools around this bay for twenty years and when the boys on the pier start talking about bait balls getting hammered in open water, you drop what you're doing.

We called this one. Said two weeks back that the building tidal flow into the new moon would sharpen up the bite at current-driven structure, and here we are — new moon was the 12th, and by the 13th the whole upper bay with peanut bunker getting pushed against the current lines off Nyatt Point and Conimicut. This isn't the herring run, that's long gone, we're way past Buckeye Brook season now. This is pure August peanut bunker, tight little schools stacking up in the rips, and stripers are using the bigger tide swings off this new moon to pin them against structure and just annihilate them.

Conimicut Light on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most reliable window. The current rips hard around that light on a big tide, and the bunker get funneled right into it. I've been throwing a 5-inch white Storm Shad or a bone-colored Super Strike Little Neck popper right into the edge of the boil and letting it sit for a second before I start working it — the fish are eating so aggressive right now that a slow twitch is plenty. Slot fish, mostly 26 to 32 inches, with the occasional overslot mixed in that'll make your reel scream. Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait, and they don't discriminate — I lost two bucktails to blues in one morning because I got lazy about checking my leader. Run 40-pound fluorocarbon minimum if you're throwing anything with a hook near those schools, because the blues are thick and hungry right now, snappers included if you're fishing close to the mouths of the coves.

Rocky Point itself has been the money spot for a shore guy with no boat. That rocky point structure holds current no matter what the tide's doing, and when the bunker get pushed up against it on an incoming tide, you get these visible boils right off the breakwater. I watched three guys hook up simultaneously Wednesday evening throwing everything from bucktails to topwater — didn't matter what was on the end of the line, the fish were eating anything that moved through the melee. That kind of chaos doesn't happen often mid-August, but the bait's been so dense this year the bass are staging early, probably getting a jump on the fall run before they'd normally show this kind of aggression.

Prudence Island's west side has been holding fish too, particularly around the ledges off the northern tip where the current squeezes between the island and the mainland. That's deeper water, 15 to 20 feet, and I've been dropping bucktails tipped with a chunk of bunker down into the seam on the last hour of the flood. Slower fishing than the blitzes up top, but more consistent — you're not relying on visible surface activity, you're just working the structure and letting the tide do the work.

Fluke are a secondary story right now but they're not absent. I've had a few decent ones, 18 to 20 inches, drifting Gulp Swimming Mullets in white and pink off the flats south of Nyatt Point in about 12 to 15 feet, moving water on the outgoing. Nothing like the doormat numbers you're hearing about from the Jersey backbays, but there's enough fluke pushing into the bay behind the warmer water to make a drift worthwhile if the blitz isn't happening.

Scup fishing has been steady and honestly underappreciated with all this bass noise. The ledges off Rocky Point and the rockpiles around Nyatt continue to produce, small pieces of squid or sandworm on a high-low rig, bottom fished in 10 to 20 feet on either side of the tide change. Not glamorous, but it's meat in the cooler when the blitz fish won't cooperate on a particular tide. Black sea bass have shown up sporadically on the deeper humps out toward Prudence, nothing you'd plan a trip around specifically but worth a few drops if you're already out there. Weakfish have been quiet — I've heard of one or two caught incidentally in the upper bay on bucktails meant for bass, but I wouldn't target them specifically right now.

Looking ahead, this peanut bunker pattern should hold as long as the bait stays dense, and with the tides still building off this new moon, I don't see a reason for it to fall apart in the next several days. If the wind stays manageable, I'd be at Conimicut or Rocky Point on that last two hours of ebb, working the edges where the current squeezes the bait. If it gets sloppy topside, drop down to bucktails and fish the structure instead of chasing the surface show. Either way, keep your leader heavy — the blues aren't going anywhere, and neither is the aggression.
